did_you_know.text: The chapter has a clear acrostic structure: the verses generally begin according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet, although the text as we have it also contains some irregularities. At the very beginning, David describes his prayer as lifting up his soul to the Lord.
Trust in the Lord is presented as protection from shame and from the enemies’ rejoicing. The verse emphasizes that trusting in the Lord also involves hoping not to fail publicly.

The verse distinguishes between “all who hope in you”—those who wait for the Lord—and “the treacherous,” whose actions are futile. This creates a contrast between hope and faithfulness on the one hand and pointless betrayal on the other.

The request for guidance is repeated in several forms: “Show me,” “Teach me,” and “Guide me.” This repetition emphasizes that the psalmist is asking not only to know the Lord’s way, but also to learn it and walk in it.

The psalmist bases his request on the Lord’s compassion and steadfast love, presenting them as qualities that are not new but have existed “from of old.” In this way, forgiveness is understood as part of the Lord’s enduring kindness.

The psalmist asks that the sins and transgressions of his youth not be remembered, and asks the Lord to remember him instead according to his steadfast love. The request does not deny the sins, but appeals to the Lord’s mercy.

The Lord is described as “good and upright,” and therefore “instructs sinners in the way.” According to the verse, the Lord’s goodness and uprightness are also expressed in guiding those who have gone astray.

The verse connects humility with receiving proper guidance: the Lord guides the humble in what is right and teaches them his way. Here, humility is presented as a quality that enables people to learn the Lord’s way.

The fear of the Lord is described as a way of life that leads to guidance: those who fear the Lord receive direction concerning the path they should choose. Later in the passage, goodness, inheriting the land, and the revelation of the covenant are also mentioned.
At the end of the chapter, the prayer shifts from the individual to the community: after personal requests for protection and deliverance, it asks the Lord to redeem Israel from all its troubles.
